readerTitle: Say the bad news in the first sentence
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관·냉난방 서비스 회사, 회계 대행 회사) · 적용 레슨: 명확한 소통 + 어려운 대화
insight: 나쁜 소식은 첫 문장에 분명히 말하고, 나머지 시간은 설득이 아니라 상대의 반응을 받아내는 데 쓴다.
misconception: 칭찬과 잡담으로 분위기를 풀어 놓은 뒤에 말해야 덜 아프다. 반발이 나오면 근거를 더 대서 납득시켜야 한다.

sources.text: Stone, D., Patton, B., & Heen, S. (1999). Difficult Conversations: How to Discuss What Matters Most. Viking/Penguin.
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 5번 카드의 '세 가지 대화(무슨 일이 있었나, 감정, 정체성)' 구분은 Stone·Patton·Heen(1999)의 틀입니다. PPL-08-03 개념 레슨의 용어와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
7번 카드 근무 시간 40시간→30시간은 가상 수치입니다. 시간 단축과 관련된 법률·계약 문제는 국가마다 달라 다루지 않았습니다. 문구가 법률 조언처럼 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.
PPL-08-01(명확한 소통)에서 '결론 먼저' 원칙을 다루는지, PPL-08-03에서 감정 인정하기를 다루는지 형제 레슨과 용어를 맞춰 주세요.

cards.title: Say the bad news in the first sentence
body: Dana owns a small plumbing and heating company. Tomorrow at 8 a.m. she has to tell Marco, her longest-serving technician, that he didn't get the lead tech job. A newer hire did.
Marco is good at his work and proud of it. Dana has rehearsed the talk three times. Every version starts with five minutes of praise.

image.label: A business owner and a technician in a van-side conversation at dawn
image.brief: 이른 아침 회사 주차장. 작업 밴 옆에서 사장(여성)이 커피 두 잔을 들고 기술자(남성)에게 다가가는 장면. 사장 표정은 긴장, 기술자는 아무것도 모르는 밝은 표정. 따뜻하지만 차분한 색감. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Dana open?
body: Marco sits down with his coffee. Dana has 20 minutes before the first job. What should her first few sentences be?

options.text: Thank him for his years of great work, then ease into the decision
options.feedback: It feels kind, but Marco hears praise and expects good news. The bigger the build-up, the harder the drop, and the praise later sounds like a setup.

options.text: "Marco, I picked Sam for the lead role. I want to tell you why, and hear how you see it."
options.feedback: This is **clear communication** at work: bottom line first, in plain words. Marco spends the talk reacting to the real news instead of guessing where it's going.

options.text: Send him an email tonight so he can take it in privately, then talk tomorrow
options.feedback: It gives him time, but a written decision with no voice behind it can feel cold. It also leaves him alone with the worst story he can imagine overnight.

cards.title: Long build-ups make bad news worse.
body: Picture Dana's original plan. Five minutes of praise. Marco relaxes and starts thinking about the raise. Then: "...but we went with Sam." Now he feels the loss *and* feels played.
People in a hard conversation stop hearing details until they know the headline. So the kindest move is to give it first, in one or two plain sentences, with no "but" hiding the point.
After that, the praise can be real. Said after the news, it reads as respect, not padding.

image.label: Two timelines: news buried at the end versus news at the start
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 두 줄. 위쪽: 'Praise, praise, small talk...' 뒤 끝에 빨간 'The news' 블록, 그 위에 놀란 얼굴 아이콘. 아래쪽: 맨 앞에 'The news' 블록, 이어서 'Why', 'Listen', 'Next steps'. 아래쪽 줄이 더 차분한 색. 간결한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Marco pushes back.
body: Marco goes quiet, then says: "That's not fair. I've been here six years. Sam's been here two."
Dana is sure the decision is right. What should she do next?

options.text: List the reasons: Sam's scheduling skills, customer reviews, training record
options.feedback: Arguing the facts right now turns it into a debate Marco has to lose. He hears "you weren't good enough," and stops listening.

options.text: "Six years matters, and I can see this stings. Tell me what's on your mind." Then listen, without reopening the decision
options.feedback: This uses **difficult conversations** thinking: name the feeling and let him speak before explaining more. The decision stays firm; his reaction gets room.

options.text: Soften it: "There may be another lead role next year"
options.feedback: It eases the moment but trades clarity for hope. If no role appears, the next talk will be much harder.

cards.title: Marco isn't arguing about facts.
body: In the *Difficult Conversations* framework, every hard talk has three layers: what happened, how people feel, and what it says about who they are.
"Six years" sounds like a fact argument. Underneath, it's the identity layer: *Am I still the senior guy here?* More evidence doesn't answer that. Being heard does.
So Dana listens first. Once Marco feels understood, he can actually take in her reasons, and she can talk about what growth looks like for him.
cards.softwareNote: In a software team the same moment shows up when a senior engineer isn't picked to lead a new project. The pushback is often about status, not the selection criteria, so a spreadsheet of reasons lands badly at first.

cards.title: Clear is not the same as blunt.
body: Leading with the news doesn't mean dropping it and walking away. Say it plainly, then stay. Pick a private place and enough time.
Don't hand out hope you can't back up, and don't pretend a decision is open when it isn't. Mixed signals feel gentle today and cruel later.
And don't over-script. A rehearsed speech can stop you from hearing what the person actually says.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You run a small bookkeeping firm. Your biggest client just left. Priya, a senior bookkeeper, will drop from 40 to 30 hours a week starting next month. You don't yet know if it's for three months or longer.

options.text: Announce it in the Monday team meeting, so everyone hears the same thing
options.feedback: It looks fair, but Priya gets personal bad news in public, with no room to react. Team news and her news are different conversations.

options.text: Meet her privately today. Say the change first, then what you know, what you don't, and when you'll know more. Then let her respond
options.feedback: Both concepts at once: **clear communication** on the headline and the unknowns, and room for the feelings that come with a pay cut.

options.text: Wait until you know how long the cut will last, so you can give her the full picture
options.feedback: A complete answer sounds better, but waiting costs her weeks of planning time. Clear means honest about the unknowns, not waiting for perfect information.

cards.softwareNote: For a SaaS company losing a large customer, the same rule holds when telling the account team their quota or roles will change: say it first, separate known from unknown, and give a date for the next update.

cards.title: Headline first, then make room.
body: You used two ideas. **Clear communication:** put the bad news in the first sentence, in plain words, and be honest about what you don't know. **Difficult conversations:** when the person pushes back, hear the feelings and identity under the words before you explain.
**Try it today:** think of one piece of bad news you've been putting off. Write the first sentence you'll say. Keep it under 20 words.
